profile.summary: Matthew presents Jesus of Nazareth as the expected Messiah, the king of Israel who fulfills the promises of the Old Testament, although differently from the expectations of many contemporaries. The gospel insists that in Jesus the reign of God erupts in history, gathering Jews and not Jews in one people, and calling the reader to a total adherence to Christ as King. The work is marked by strong continuity with the Scriptures of Israel, a broad view of God's people and a constant appeal to obedient discipleship.
profile.setting: The introduction places the gospel in a primitive Christian community near Jerusalem, in intense contact and daily with Jews who remained firmly attached to the Torah. The scenario seems to be a moment of decision: would this community continue as an internal group to Judaism or distinguish itself from it as a separate faith? In this environment, the Christians who read Matthew faced religious, social, ritual and political pressures, and needed to learn to follow Jesus as Christian Jews amid debates about the law, the identity of the Messiah, the legitimate leadership of God's people and the relationship of the Gentiles with the church and Israel. As for authorship and date, the ancient tradition attributes the gospel to the apostle Matthew, but the relationship with Mark's material, the exact form of composition and the place of writing remain discussed. The likely date is between 65 and 80 AD, with Antioch of Syria as a hypothesis often considered plausible.

structure.label: Introduction and identity of Jesus
structure.description: Birth, initial threats and presentation of Jesus as the promised Messiah, in continuity with the hope of Israel.

structure.label: Founding teaching of the Kingdom
structure.description: The great teaching block in which Jesus exposes the righteousness of the Kingdom and defines the demands of discipleship.

structure.label: Power of Jesus and sending the disciples
structure.description: Miracles confirming the authority of Jesus and sending the twelve to extend his mission.

structure.label: Varied responses and increasing rejection
structure.description: Israel's reaction to Jesus" ministry, including opposition, misunderstanding and increasing conflict.

structure.label: Final confrontation, denunciations and judgment
structure.description: Jesus confronts leaders and authorities, announces solemn warnings and speaks of God's judgment on Jerusalem.

structure.label: Passion, Resurrection and Final Commission
structure.description: Arrested, judgment and crucifixion, followed by the vindication in the resurrection and the universal mission to the disciples.

readingKeys: Notice how Matthew links episodes of Jesus" life to promises and standards of the Scriptures of Israel.
Note the alternation between teaching and narrative, and how each block deepens the identity of Jesus and the demands of discipleship.
Pay attention to the contrasts between the positive reaction of some, the rejection of many and the opening of the mission to the nations.
profile.cautions: This introduction recognizes that authorship, the exact date, the place of composition and the immediate audience of Matthew are questions discussed. Thus, the reader should deal with these conclusions as probable, not absolute. It is also important to remember that the portrait of Matthew's community is inferred from the gospel itself, not from direct external documentation.

dossier.narratedEra: The gospel narrates the life of Jesus of Nazareth in its first century Jewish context, since his genealogy and birth (Mt 1-2), through his ministry in Galilee and Judea, to his crucifixion, resurrection and final commission (Mt 26-28). The notes put him before a world dominated by Jewish and Roman authorities, by debates about the Law, the temple, the messiah and the identity of the people of God.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition is treated as after the narrated events. The introductory notes indicate that Matthew was probably written between AD 65 and 80, with many interpreters preferring a date after AD 70 if the author used Mark as a source; others defend earlier date, until the 1950s. The most frequently suggested location is Antioch of Syria, although this is presented as a probable proposal and not certainty. The ancient tradition attributed the work to the apostle Matthew, and the aforementioned academic discussion also involves the relationship with Mark and the possibility of a specific Jewish-Christian audience or a wider audience.

politics.title: Herod Antipas as tetrarch of Galilee and Pereia
politics.detail: Mt 14:1 presents Herod Antipas with official title of tetrarch, that is, ruler of a fourth part of the kingdom, over Galilee and Perea. The notes place his government between 4 BC and AD 39 and link his action against John the Baptist to a real political context of repression.
politics.readingImpact: When reading the arrest and execution of John, the reader realizes that the conflict is not only moral or religious; there is also political risk when the prophetic message confronts local rulers.

politics.title: John's execution as a public threat to power
politics.detail: The notes claim that the popularity of John's message posed a political threat and recall the later Jewish interpretation of Herod Antipas' military defeat before Aretas in AD 36 as judgment for having killed an innocent.
politics.readingImpact: This gives the episode a burden of public denunciation: John's death is not mere biographical detail, but an example of how the prophetic truth collides with the stability of power.

politics.title: Disputes on legitimate leadership of God's people
politics.detail: The introduction highlights internal debates between Christians and Jews about who are the true leaders of God's people, citing passages as Mt 4:18-22; 10:2-4; 21:43; 23:1-36; 28:16-20. The emphasis is that the authority of Jesus displaces existing leaderships.
politics.readingImpact: The gospel should be read as a confrontation of authority: Jesus not only teaches, but redefines who rules and leads the people of God.

politics.title: Rome and the world of nations
politics.detail: The introduction says that the disciples would be sent to evangelize the Roman world, and Mt 28:19 speaks of the mission to all nations. This places the gospel in an imperial horizon wider than Israel.
politics.readingImpact: Reading gains missionary and political reach: the lordship of Jesus is announced in contrast to any universal pretense of Rome.

politics.title: The plot of Jerusalem and the judgment on the city
politics.detail: Tyndale's introduction summarizes that Jesus predicts the destruction of Jerusalem (Mt 24-25). The work therefore includes a historical judgment dimension on the city and its authorities.
politics.readingImpact: The reader must realize that the warnings of Jesus have a concrete historical dimension, not just symbolic or spiritual.

customs.title: Noivado as permanent legal bond
customs.detail: In Mt 1:18-19, the notes explain that the Jewish engagement was a permanent relationship, which was imprisoned only by legal process, so that Mary was already considered Joseph's wife. It is also observed that Joseph, as a fairman, could publicly expose Mary or dissolve the commitment in secret.
customs.readingImpact: The virgin birth is read within a real legal framework, which intensifies the social cost of Joseph's obedience and Mary's vulnerability.

customs.title: Honour, shame and legal discipline in cases of suspected adultery
customs.detail: The note at Mt 1:19 mentions that Joseph could expose Mary to the public trial, evoking Deut 22:23-27 and Num 5:11-31, or choose to break the engagement silently. The contrast highlights his mercy.
customs.readingImpact: The context helps to read Joseph's decision as an act of justice tempered by compassion, not as passivity.

customs.title: Food refuses, tables and hospitality around Jesus
customs.detail: The introduction describes the Judeo-Christian community in daily coexistence with Jews committed to the Torah, and the story of Matthew 9:10-13 presupposes a meal with friends of Matthew and Jesus. The gospel thus preserves the social environment of the table as a space of relationship and conflict.
customs.readingImpact: Meals appear as places of inclusion and moral dispute; Jesus sits with people seen as problematic by the religious sectors.

customs.title: Dance practices and heroic elite banquet
customs.detail: Mt 14:6-8 describes the dance of Herodias' daughter and the request of John's head on a tray. The notes note that sexually provocative dances were common in corrupted cuts and that the presentation of a head on a tray was not unknown in the ancient world.
customs.readingImpact: The account becomes more vivid and gloomy: the banquet of the elite becomes the scene of humiliation and ritualized violence.

customs.title: Baptism as Public Identification with Jesus
customs.detail: In Mt 28:19, baptism is explained as public identification and handing over to Jesus and to the work of salvation. The language of "in name" indicates entry in a relationship with its benefits.
customs.readingImpact: The missionary order is not only doctrinal instruction; it involves public rite of adherence and change of loyalty.

customs.title: Testimony of women and their social assessment
customs.detail: In Mt 28:1, the mention of two women as witnesses is highlighted as a relevant detail to historical credibility, because the female witness was considered less reliable than the male in certain ancient contexts.
customs.readingImpact: The gospel preserves an uncomfortable narrative trait, which in the notes reinforces the seriousness of tradition over the empty tomb.

language.title: Structure in kiosm in genealogy
language.detail: In Mt 1:1, the notes note that the names Jesus, David, and Abraham reappear in reverse order in the genealogy, forming a kiosm. This literary arrangement highlights theological connections, not just a genealogical list.
language.readingImpact: The reader is led to view genealogy as literary argumentation: Jesus is presented deliberately as a fulfillment of the Davidic line and the promise to Abraham.

language.title: Gematria of David's name
language.detail: In Mt 1:17, the division into fourteen generations is explained as possible numerical emphasis linked to the gematria of the name "Davi." The note understands this as a strategy to underline the Messianic credentials of Jesus.
language.readingImpact: The reading of the genealogy begins to show theological and memorial intention: the numerical form itself reinforces that Jesus is the Davidic Messiah.

language.title: Kingdom of the heavens as a Jewish circumloquium
language.detail: The introduction states that the expression "Kingdom of Heaven" is an indirect way, used by Matthew, to say "Kingdom of God." Notes associate this language with promises of the OT, current presence, divine power, judgment, and final consummation.
language.readingImpact: The reader must realize that Matthew preserves Jewish sensitivity in vocabulary while insisting on the full scope of God's rule.

language.title: "Here I am here" and the divine self-identification
language.detail: In Mt 14:27, the speech of Jesus is translated literally as I am, and the note relates it to manifestations of God and to Ex 3:14. The effect is to present Jesus in the language of divine revelation.
language.readingImpact: In the episode of the sea, the reader sees not only the courage of Jesus, but a clue of his divine identity and sovereign authority.

language.title: Language of TA fulfillment as distinctive trait
language.detail: The introduction says that Matthew is marked by repeated links between Old Testament texts and the life of Jesus, in a Jewish commentary style. In Mt 1:22-23, for example, Isaiah 7:14 is read as a fulfillment at the virgin birth.
language.readingImpact: This technique forces the reader to read Jesus in continuity with the ancient faith of Israel, without reducing the gospel to an isolated biography.

language.title: Make disciples" as a central command
language.detail: In Mt 28:19-20, the note explains that the main imperative is "making disciples," while "indo" functions as a participle of support. Disciple is defined as one who repents, trusts in Jesus for salvation and obeys his teachings.
language.readingImpact: The verbal form guides the mission of the church: evangelization and teaching go together, not as separate stages.

timeline.title: Genealogy and the birth of Jesus as an initial fulfillment
timeline.detail: Mt 1-2 is presented as a section in which lineage, birth, and geography of Jesus" childhood meet expectations of the OT, while human attempts to thwart God's plan fail. The focus is on the beginning of the Messianic history, not in a detailed external chronology.
timeline.readingImpact: The beginning of the gospel already frames the life of Jesus as divine fulfillment and vain resistance against the will of God.

timeline.title: Brief ministry of Jesus and his sequence of actions
timeline.detail: The introduction summarizes the public ministry of Jesus in sequence: proclamation of the righteousness of God, miracles, sending of the twelve, rejection, final confrontations, passion, death, resurrection and commission. This organizes the reading of the book as a compact historical-theological narrative.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader accompanies the gospel as a coherent progression, and not as a loose collection of episodes.

timeline.title: Writing context between AD 65 and 80
timeline.detail: The section "Date and Location" places Matthew's composition probably between AD 65 and 80, with debate about whether or not to depend on Mark and, consequently, whether the date would be post-70 or earlier. There is also a chance of a date in the 1950s, but it appears as a minority.
timeline.readingImpact: This prevents confusing the time of writing with the narrated time; the gospel reflects debates after Jesus" ministry.

timeline.title: Fall of Jerusalem as an implicit horizon
timeline.detail: The introduction understands that Mt 2425 provides for judgment and destruction of Jerusalem, which connects the gospel to a historical horizon of Jewish crisis and discernment of Israel's future.
timeline.readingImpact: The eschatological warnings gain historical and pastoral weight, not merely abstract.

timeline.title: Post-ascension and ancient tradition about Matthew
timeline.detail: Matthew Henry claims that the gospel was written about eight years after the ascension, although this is an ancient tradition and not a proven date in the notes. Tyndale also records the tradition that Matthew would have moved to evangelize India in the 1960s of the 1st century, according to Eusebius.
timeline.readingImpact: Reading is informed by tradition and not documentary certainty; it is appropriate to distinguish the old testimony from the probable date proposed by modern criticism.

timeline.title: Resurrection and mission to nations
timeline.detail: Mt 28 is treated as the historical-theological climax of the gospel: empty tomb, apparitions, attempt to discredit the resurrection and the final commission. The mission to nations is presented as the formal beginning of expansion beyond Israel.
timeline.readingImpact: The outcome of the book shifts the story of Jesus to the history of the church and its worldwide mission.

investigation: The traditional authorship identifies the apostle Matthew, but the notes also mention modern debates about Mark's dependence on the use or not of a Hebrew/Amass previous version.
The location in Antioch of Syria is presented as probable, but not decisive; the source does not provide conclusive proof.

There is interpretive tension on the original audience: community still within Judaism, already separated from it, or wider audience. The notes themselves recognize serious debate and suggest caution.
The use of early date (years 50) or late (after AD 70) is treated as debated, depending on the relationship with Marks and internal inferences.
Matthew Henry offers strong chronology and assertions about the primitive reception of the four gospels, but this reflects traditional/devotional reading, not independent historical demonstration.

Data on Herod Antipas, Aretas and the practice of placing a head in a tray comes from the secondary notes and serve to contextualize Mt 14, not for exhaustive reconstruction of the political history of the period.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the notes provided and, therefore, is selective: it privileges explicitly discussed statements about Jewish-Christian context, composition, heroic politics, social customs and literary language. There were no gaps with external reconstructions or speculative chronologies. Some questions remain controversial in their own sources, especially authorship, original language, exact date, place of composition and extension of the target audience. There is also unequal coverage: chapters 1, 14 and 28 receive more detail because the attached sources comment them more directly. Where the notes make inferences, they were marked as interpretation; where they record debate, this was maintained without solving the issue.
